best.rationale: y1 connects attacker-side scaling (ref-024), latent safety elicited through BoN (ref-007), and adaptive compute allocation (ref-002) through a concrete experiment measuring attack success over attacker and defender budgets. That surface could directly inform defense spending, even if the proposed power-law relationship fails. Its claim that ref-024 assumes exactly one defender sample is not established by the abstract. x2 addresses a useful combination of ref-002, ref-004, and ref-012, but leaves the integration of pessimistic rejection sampling and augmented-reward reranking unclear. It also does not explain why reward uncertainty measures prompt difficulty or how adaptive budgets affect constraint calibration. y1 offers a clearer experiment and more interpretable outcome.

worst.rationale: x1 does not establish its gap against ref-004, which already relates policy coverage to inference-time alignment performance, compute, and reward hacking. Omitting that closest reference materially weakens its grounding. It also leaves the reward-optimal distribution and assumptions connecting KL divergence, Pearson correlation, and gold-reward bounds unspecified; a Gaussian demonstration would not establish the broader claim. y2 has serious weaknesses: ensemble spread is not established as a calibrated upper confidence bound, MBR proximity does not itself establish cost uncertainty, and simultaneous gold safety and helpfulness monotonicity is ambitious. Nevertheless, robustness to imperfect safety costs is a recognizable, scoped extension of ref-012 and ref-004.

diversity.rationale: X contains a theoretical coverage proposal, but x2 and x3 substantially overlap in adapting sampling budgets for safety using reward-based selection and calibration. Y separates a two-sided attacker–defender compute study, a constrained selection algorithm, and an empirical study of guard overoptimization. Although y2 and y3 share concerns about imperfect cost models, their interventions and experimental questions differ meaningfully.

overall.rationale: Y provides a stronger leading experiment and more distinct research choices. y3 offers concrete sweeps of selection pressure, guard models, and proxy–evaluator disagreement, grounded in ref-006, ref-005, ref-016, and ref-021. Its claim that earlier overoptimization work concerns only helpfulness is unsupported, and over-refusal should be separated from harmfulness degradation. These qualifications still leave a useful empirical question. In X, x3 adds less beyond x2, leaves difficulty classification undefined, and mischaracterizes ref-012's dual-variable calibration as reward-model calibration. Its guard-model baselines also need an explicit deployment protocol. Across the available choices, Y better supports selecting a useful, testable project.
